summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would create an Anti-Dumping Commission within the Australian Customs and Border Protection Service, led by a Commissioner and supported by Customs staff.
It would transfer the Customs chief executive officer's existing anti-dumping responsibilities and powers to the Commissioner, with staff assisting under the Commissioner's direction.
Transitional rules would transfer relevant pending court and tribunal cases to the Commissioner, and the bill's proposed commencement date is 1 July 2013.
changes: The minister could appoint a full-time or part-time Commissioner for a term of up to five years.
The Commissioner would have to report interests that conflict, or could conflict, with official functions to the minister in writing.
A full-time Commissioner would need ministerial approval for outside paid work, while a part-time Commissioner could not undertake work the minister considers conflicting.
The Commissioner could delegate functions and powers to Customs officers, who would have to follow the Commissioner's written directions.
The Commissioner would come under the oversight of the Integrity Commissioner and the Australian Commission for Law Enforcement Integrity.
summary.affected: The Commissioner, Customs staff, the responsible minister and the Australian Commission for Law Enforcement Integrity are affected.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Supported the Customs Amendment (Anti-Dumping Commission) Bill 2013, accusing the opposition of having opposed the $300 million Steel Transformation Plan, a $5.4 billion new car plant assistance package, and a $1 billion clean technology program while claiming to support manufacturing workers.

speeches.speaker: John Cobb
speeches.brief: Supported the anti-dumping bill as an adoption of coalition policy released in November 2011, illustrating the problem with the tomato processing industry, where 400 growers once supplied seven canneries but now only about nine growers supply a single processor due to subsidised Italian imports.

speeches.speaker: Sharman Stone
speeches.brief: Supported the anti-dumping bill in principle but questioned whether the promised $24.4 million in funding would actually materialise, citing a $2.8 billion excess of food and beverage imports over exports in the 2011-12 financial year and a rally of 600 dairy farmers in Tongala struggling against underpriced imports.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: Supported the anti-dumping bill, which increases Customs funding by $24.4 million and nearly doubles investigator numbers, citing solar panel maker Tindo Solar in his electorate as a local manufacturer struggling to compete against Chinese panels allegedly dumped below cost, and noted about 8,000 people in his electorate work in manufacturing.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: Supported anti-dumping measures but warned the carbon tax makes Australian producers less competitive, and criticised government cuts including $64.1 million and 750 staff from Customs, arguing this undermines Australia's biosecurity and clean, green reputation.

speeches.speaker: Michael McCormack
speeches.brief: Supported the anti-dumping bill, citing constituent complaints that cheap Chinese apple juice concentrate is undercutting local apple growers and that Labor increased the annual export registration charge for packing sheds from $550 to $8,530, and described citrus growers dumping fruit after being offered as little as $25 a tonne for navel oranges.

speeches.speaker: Michael McCormack
speeches.brief: Supported the Customs Amendment (Anti-Dumping Commission) Bill 2013 but linked it to the case for more dams, noting Australia uses just six per cent of its available water resources, three per cent less than the world average, and argued matching world-average water use could double food production to feed more than 100 million people, while doubting where the government's promised $24.4 million in antidumping funding would come from.

speeches.speaker: Jason Clare
speeches.brief: Responded that the Customs Amendment (Anti-Dumping Commission) Bill 2013 implements the Brumby review's recommendation to create an Australian Anti-Dumping Commission inside Customs, rejected opposition claims it mirrors Liberal Party policy, which would instead move responsibility to the Department of Industry, and said the bill was the fifth of five reform tranches backed by over $24 million in extra funding.

speeches.speaker: Richard Colbeck
speeches.brief: The coalition supported the Customs Amendment (Anti-Dumping Commission) Bill 2013 to establish the Australian Anti-Dumping Commission, but criticised the government for belatedly adopting opposition policy and raised concerns about the source of $24.4 million in funding, citing failed anti-dumping cases that cost jobs at Kimberly-Clark, SPC Ardmona and CSR Viridian.
